title: JPMorgan Stock And Other US Large Caps Built For Less Frequent Earnings Reports - simplywall.st
content:
When regulators rethink how often companies report earnings, information becomes the key asset. A shift toward semi-annual reporting could reward large, financially solid businesses that already keep investors updated between results, and expose those that rely on the minimum disclosure rules. This article looks at how that debate around shorter reporting cycles and continuous updates intersects with one specific corner of the market, large cap US stocks with strong corporate governance. Below, you will find 3 stocks from this screener that appear well positioned to handle thinner reporting calendars by keeping investors informed in real time. Overview: JPMorgan Chase is a global financial services company that provides consumer and commercial banking, investment banking, markets, and asset and wealth management services to individuals, businesses, institutions, and governments across major regions worldwide. Operations: JPMorgan Chase generates most of its revenue from Consumer & Community Banking at about US$67.7b and Commercial and Investment Bank at about US$85.4b. Asset & Wealth Management contributes around US$25.8b, partially offset by smaller corporate and tax-equivalent adjustments. Investors looking at JPMorgan Chase in the context of stronger corporate governance and a possible shift to semi-annual reporting may find its size, breadth and disclosure habits especially important. The bank combines global scale across consumer banking, payments and markets with high-quality earnings and a long record of detailed communication that can help reduce information gaps if formal updates become less frequent. At the same time, tighter regulation, fintech competition and insider selling are real watchpoints that could affect growth and valuation. How JPMorgan uses its capital strength, AI spending and fee-driven businesses to balance these pressures is central to the story, and there is more beneath the surface than headline earnings or a single P/E can show. JPMorgan’s large balance sheet and frequent communication may obscure where the real pressure lies. It is therefore helpful to view everything in one place with the 3 key rewards and 1 important warning sign Overview: Cintas provides corporate uniforms and a wide range of workplace services, from rental garments and facility supplies to first aid, safety and fire protection products, serving everyone from small local businesses to large corporations across the US, Canada and Latin America. Operations: Cintas generates most of its revenue from Uniform Rental and Facility Services at about US$8.6b, with additional contributions from First Aid and Safety Services of roughly US$1.4b and about US$1.3b from other activities. Cintas attracts attention in a world of potentially less frequent earnings reports because it already runs on contract driven, recurring revenue and emphasizes long term customer relationships, which can make its business easier to understand between formal updates. High profitability, including a net margin near 18% and return on equity around 39%, sits alongside strong governance, disciplined management pay and recognition such as TIME America’s Best Companies, all of which can support investor trust if reporting cycles stretch out. On the flip side, high debt, sensitivity to trends like remote work that could reduce uniform demand, and pending regulatory review of the UniFirst acquisition are important issues to watch, and the current P/E leaves little room for disappointment. High margins and rich contracts make Cintas look like a steady compounder, but the real story may lie in how those numbers compare with its balance sheet and acquisition risk, which the analysis report for Cintas begins to examine. Overview: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, running global platforms such as Search, YouTube, Android, Chrome and Google Play, alongside Google Cloud and a portfolio of earlier stage projects in areas like self driving cars and internet infrastructure. Alphabet stands out in a potential shift to semi annual reporting because it already runs on frequent, detailed updates, a high quality board and a long history of explaining complex businesses like Search, YouTube and Google Cloud in plain terms. The company combines strong earnings growth, expanding margins around 54.8% and a rapidly growing Google Cloud backlog tied to AI infrastructure. It still trades on a P/E that is described as good value versus its peer group. At the same time, heavy AI capex, high reliance on external funding sources and ongoing global antitrust pressure keep risk firmly on the table, which makes understanding what investors might be missing in the numbers especially important. Alphabet’s expanding margins and AI heavy Google Cloud backlog hint that the real story is still unfolding, and the analyst forecasts for Alphabet could show where expectations may be quietly stretching further than most realize. title: Citi, JPM Reportedly In Talks To Join OpenAI IPO Bank Lineup - Stocktwits
content: OpenAI is reportedly in talks with banks including Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM) to work on its upcoming initial public offering (IPO). A confidential IPO filing from the ChatGPT maker is reportedly expected within weeks. The listing would put OpenAI ahead of rival artificial intelligence firm Anthropic PBC, which is also preparing for a potential offering later this year or early next. Citigroup and JPMorgan may join Goldman Sachs (GS) and Morgan Stanley (MS) in preparing OpenAI’s listing, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are already working with the company on a draft IPO prospectus that is expected to be filed confidentially with regulators soon. Adding more banks as underwriters would bring OpenAI closer to a potential IPO, which could be filed in the coming weeks, Bloomberg reported. However, the talks are still ongoing and may not lead to Citigroup and JPMorgan being included, with other banks also expected to participate. OpenAI, led by Sam Altman, is targeting a possible public listing as early as September, though the plans remain fluid and subject to change, according to a Wall Street Journal report. OpenAI’s IPO would come after Elon Musk’s SpaceX listing, expected to be the largest ever at around $75 billion, and ahead of rival AI firm Anthropic, which is also planning a large public offering later this year or early next year, stated the Bloomberg report. Over the past year, competition in artificial intelligence has intensified, especially from Anthropic. However, OpenAI continues to expand rapidly, driven by strong growth in its AI agent tools and increasing adoption among enterprise customers. On Thursday, Anthropic said it raised $65 billion in a funding round that valued the company at $965 billion, surpassing OpenAI’s most recent valuation of $852 billion. Shares of Oculis Holding (OCS) fell more than 23% during Friday afternoon trading after the company reported topline results from its Phase 3 DIAMOND-1 and DIAMOND-2 trials of OCS-01 eye drops in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME). The company said the primary endpoint of the Phase 3 studies was not met. At the time of writing, OCS shares were down 23.42%. The DIAMOND program included two Phase 3 clinical trials testing OCS-01 eye drops in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) over 52 weeks. More than 800 patients were enrolled across 119 study sites in the U.S. and other countries. The main goal of the trials, which was to improve vision as measured by best corrected visual acuity, was not met in either study. However, the treatment did show a clear benefit on a secondary measure, with OCS-01 reducing retinal thickness compared to the placebo group across both trials. Based on the trial results, Oculis said it will not move forward with an FDA filing for OCS-01 in diabetic macular edema at this time. Riad Sherif, M.D., Chief Executive Officer of Oculis, said, “We are naturally disappointed that the substantial and sustained reduction in retinal thickness observed across both trials didn’t translate into BCVA improvement at week 52.” Now, the company will redirect its focus and resources to other late-stage programs, including the Privosegtor PIONEER trial for optic neuropathies and the Licaminlimab PREDICT-1 study in dry eye disease. Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) reported new data from a lung cancer study, showing that patients treated with its intravenous RYBREVANT in combination with LAZCLUZE lived for a median of nearly 3.5 years. The results were presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting. Despite the positive study update, Johnson & Johnson shares were down 2.3% during Friday afternoon trading. JNJ said the updated results from its Phase 1/1b CHRYSALIS-2 study add to growing evidence supporting the use of the drug combination in patients with both common and atypical EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Joel Neal, the study's principal investigator and a professor of medicine at Stanford Medicine, said treatment options for patients with atypical EGFR-mutated NSCLC remain limited, with questions still surrounding the effectiveness of existing therapies. “The responses we've seen in this trial suggest the potential for more durable disease control, and the overall survival data reinforce that picture,” Neal said. He added that the long-term results could help shape future treatment decisions for this subtype of lung cancer. Johnson & Johnson evaluated RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE as a first-line treatment in 49 patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carrying atypical EGFR mutations. More than one-third of the patients had multiple atypical mutations. The latest data showed patients treated with the combination achieved a median overall survival of 41 months, or nearly 3.5 years. Survival rates remained strong over time, with 55% of patients alive after three years and 46% alive after four years. CHRYSALIS-2 is a Phase 1/1b study testing LAZCLUZE alone and in combination with RYBREVANT in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer. A total of 460 patients were enrolled in the trial. Shares of Rio Tinto (RIO) were up in morning trade after the company announced that it has started commissioning its $1.5-billion AP60 smelter expansion at Complexe Arvida in Quebec. This marks a major milestone for the deployment of its state-of-the-art, low-carbon aluminium smelting technology. At the time of writing, RIO stocks had gained around 1%. The commissioning process is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. Once fully operational, the expansion will add around 160,000 metric tonnes of annual primary aluminum production capacity, bringing total output using AP60 technology to about 220,000 metric tonnes per year. The project is expected to support around 100 permanent jobs in the region. During peak construction, it created more than 1,500 jobs and generated over $1 billion in economic benefits for Quebec. Rio Tinto said the expansion marks a new chapter in its long-standing presence in Quebec and will strengthen its ability to supply North American customers with low-carbon aluminum used in transportation, construction, electrical applications and consumer products. Rio Tinto said its AP60 technology is among the most efficient and low-carbon aluminum production technologies available at commercial scale. Powered by hydropower in Canada, the technology produces about one-sixth of the greenhouse gas emissions of the industry average and roughly half the emissions of the older technology used at the nearby Arvida smelter. The company also expects the AP60 expansion to reduce fine particulate matter emissions by up to 90%. Shares of Firefly Aerospace (FLY) rose over 1% in overnight trading heading into Friday, shrugging off a discounted stock offering as investors focused on a growing list of catalysts, including fresh NASA lunar contracts and a setback for rival Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket program. FLY stock fell nearly 14% on Thursday, logging its worst session in over six months, with shares on track to three straight weeks of gains. However, shares are looking to record a third consecutive month in the green. Late Thursday, Firefly priced its public offering at $48 per share, representing a 3% discount to the stock’s last closing price. The offering consists of 12 million shares in total, including 4 million newly issued shares from Firefly and 8 million shares being sold by existing stockholders. Additionally, the selling stockholders granted underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to 1.8 million additional shares at the public offering price, less underwriting discounts and commissions. Firefly said it plans to use proceeds from its portion of the offering for general corporate purposes, including supporting growth initiatives and recently awarded programs. Earlier this week, the company announced a $75 million subcontract from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory to support the agency's MoonFall mission, part of NASA's broader Moon Base initiative. Under the agreement, Firefly's Elytra spacecraft will transport four autonomous drones to the Moon's south pole, where they will survey terrain, explore permanently shadowed regions and help identify resources such as water ice that could support future human missions. The award expands Firefly's growing lunar portfolio, which already includes multiple Blue Ghost missions under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services program. The company recently completed key testing milestones for Blue Ghost Mission 2 and continues advancing Missions 3 and 4 while expanding spacecraft production capabilities. The contract was announced alongside NASA's first phase of its Moon Base initiative, which is expected to include 25 launches, 21 lunar landings and four metric tons of cargo delivered to the Moon. Firefly was selected to deploy the first drones to the lunar surface using its Elytra spacecraft, while Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 cargo lander to deliver future lunar rovers. Other awards went to Lunar Outpost and Astrolab for rover development. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has also outlined plans to invest over $20 billion over the next seven years in lunar infrastructure as part of the agency's Moon Base and Artemis programs, which aim to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon later this decade. title: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon Just Sent an Ominous Warning to Wall Street: "Close to as Good as It Gets" - The Globe and Mail
content: JPMorgan Chase just posted incredibly strong earnings. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said he has concerns about a range of issues affecting the market and economy. There aren't too many people in the financial world more respected than JPMorgan Chase Chief Executive Officer Jamie Dimon. JPMorgan Chase is the largest bank in the U.S. by assets, and Dimon has successfully steered the company through the Great Recession and the pandemic, all while making some very smart strategic moves along the way. Notably, JPMorgan acquired First Republic as it was on the brink of failure during the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank crisis. Needless to say, investors and stakeholders across Wall Street are closely listening to Dimon's comments on the economy and markets. Where to invest $1,000 right now? Our analyst team just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks to buy right now, when you join Stock Advisor. See the stocks » Recently, Dimon just sent an ominous warning to Wall Street, telling analysts during JPMorgan's second-quarter earnings conference call, "It's getting close to as good as it gets." JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. Image source: JPMorgan Chase. When Dimon said that, he was referring to the bank's splendid second-quarter earnings, in which every business line achieved record revenue, and the company generated a 23% core return on tangible common equity (ROTCE). The bank has issued a long-term target of 17% ROTCE yet exceeded it in each of the past five quarters. A bank like JPMorgan is highly reflective of the U.S. economy, so a blowout quarter like the one JPMorgan just had at least partially reflects this. Still, Dimon has long had concerns about many of the issues affecting markets during the past few years. "I do think those risks are probably bigger than other people think," he said in a July 20 CNBC interview, referring to geopolitical risks and rising government deficits that the current administration is seemingly ignoring as it ramps up military spending using borrowed money. But in another podcast, Dimon also acknowledged that the global economy has become more resilient due to its reduced dependence on energy, so even a renewed escalation between the U.S. and Iran may not derail the U.S. economy and stock market. Dimon also said he would not personally buy long-maturity U.S. Treasury bonds because he believes a group of bond investors, known as the bond vigilantes, will demand higher yields to compensate for the risk associated with the U.S. government's growing debt. Additionally, Dimon expressed caution about the broader market's elevated valuation and the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, at least in the near term. Dimon said, alluding to the fact that the big winners of the internet were not the dominant early pioneers: The amount of money being spent is huge. Will it, in total, pay off? Probably, just like the internet did. Will it pay off the way you expect and the timetable you expect? Definitely not. Dimon is extremely savvy and widely viewed as the best CEO in banking, but he often strikes a note of cautious. It's a tone he's frequently had since the pandemic, and it has served the him well throughout his career. Nonetheless, Dimon is issuing Wall Street an ominous warning, particularly about market froth and the state of the U.S. government's finances. The U.S. continues to rack up significant debt, which takes a big bite out of its budget through annual interest payments. How long can this continue without any consequences? It's hard to say, but investors should not be complacent. I think the high debt has already had significant consequences, given that the money being printed has likely inflated asset prices and contributed to affordability issues and the wealth gap in the U.S. Investors should also heed Dimon's advice on AI. Just because companies like OpenAI and Anthropic dominate the landscape right now, that doesn't guarantee their success. They may be the forerunners of the real winners down the road. title: JPMorgan cuts Rollins to Neutral on demand uncertainty, slashes price target - Yahoo! Finance Canada
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Investing.com -- JPMorgan downgraded Rollins to Neutral from Overweight and cut its price target to $45 from $70, saying uncertainty around weakening residential demand and a slower-than-expected margin recovery has made the pest control company's near-term risk-reward less compelling despite its intact long-term growth story. The brokerage said questions raised at Rollins' investor day outweighed the answers, particularly around the sharp slowdown in consumer-initiated demand and the timing of a margin recovery. Management said demand patterns had become more volatile than at any point in nearly a decade, while noting customer retention remained strong and suggesting changes in AI-powered search could be affecting lead generation, though the impact remains difficult to quantify. JPMorgan analyst Tomohiko Sano lowered fiscal 2026 and 2027 revenue growth forecasts to 8.7% and 8.4%, respectively, while reducing adjusted EBITDA margin estimates to 21.9% and 22.2%. The brokerage also cut adjusted EPS estimates to $1.17 for 2026 and $1.26 for 2027. The downgrade follows a weaker-than-expected second quarter, with revenue and margins missing expectations as residential brands dependent on search, digital marketing and inbound calls saw declining lead volumes. Residential organic growth slowed to 3.6%, while recurring revenue and relationship-driven businesses such as HomeTeam and Fox remained more resilient. JPMorgan said Rollins entered the peak season with a cost structure built for stronger growth, leading to profitability pressure as demand softened. Management has lowered its 2026 incremental EBITDA margin target to at least 10% from its longer-term framework of 30%-35%, although it expects improvement to be weighted toward the fourth quarter and reaffirmed confidence in its long-term growth algorithm. title: Why is JPMorgan Chase Expanding its Branch Network in a Digital Age - Kavout | AI
content: JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), the largest U.S. bank, is embarking on an ambitious physical expansion, planning to open over 160 new branches across 30+ states in 2026 and aiming for 500 new locations by 2027. This strategy appears to defy the broader industry trend of branch closures, with competitors like Bank of America and Wells Fargo having significantly reduced their physical footprints. The bank's leadership believes that a robust physical presence remains a critical component of its long-term growth, even as digital banking continues its rapid ascent. This move is part of a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar investment to grow and modernize its branch network, including renovating 1,700 existing locations. The goal isn't merely to add more brick-and-mortar; it's a strategic play to deepen customer relationships, enhance cross-selling opportunities, and extend the bank's reach into new and underserved markets. JPMorgan's approach is a calculated bet on a hybrid model, combining its top-ranked digital platform with an accessible physical footprint to capture a wider array of customer needs. The market's initial reaction to this aggressive spending, alongside significant AI investments, was notably negative. Following its Q4 2025 earnings report on January 13, 2026, JPM shares fell 3.8% in a single day, primarily due to an "expense shock" in its 2026 guidance. Management projected expenses to balloon to $105 billion this year, up from $96 billion in 2025. This substantial increase, driven by both AI and physical expansion, signals a period of heavy investment that could weigh on short-term profitability but is designed to fortify the bank's position for the future. Despite the short-term market jitters, JPMorgan's leadership, under CEO Jamie Dimon, has historically used periods of uncertainty to consolidate power and invest for the long haul. The current strategy aligns with this "fortress" mentality, aiming to ensure the bank remains a dominant force, capable of weathering economic shifts and capitalizing on flight-to-quality dynamics during potential market corrections. This expansion is not a retreat from digital, but rather a complementary effort to serve diverse customer segments more effectively. JPMorgan's decision to double down on physical branches is a nuanced strategy, recognizing that while digital channels handle the bulk of routine transactions, human interaction remains crucial for complex financial needs and relationship building. The bank's data indicates that branches are highly effective in driving growth, reporting a 30% increase in consumer and small business customers between 2019 and 2022, and an impressive $85 billion in deposit growth from branches since 2017. This suggests that physical locations are not obsolete but are evolving into advisory hubs. The bank is employing a highly segmented strategy, tailoring branch designs and services to specific customer types. For instance, J.P. Morgan Financial Centers offer concierge-style service for affluent and high-net-worth clients, featuring private meeting spaces and premium finishes. These centers, with 21 currently operating and 10 more planned by year-end 2026, aim to deepen relationships and unlock cross-selling opportunities across mortgages, auto loans, investment products, and credit cards. This premium model mirrors Apple's successful retail strategy, where physical stores serve as brand experience centers rather than mere transaction points. Beyond affluent markets, Chase is also expanding into low-to-moderate income (LMI) and rural communities with "Community Centers." These centers are designed for community gatherings, financial health workshops, and small business pop-ups, staffed by Community Managers who provide financial education and support. This dual-pronged approach allows JPMorgan to capture both high-value and emerging market segments, aiming for 75% of Americans to be within a reasonable drive of a branch and over 50% within each state. The bank also reported a 20% productivity increase by bankers since 2019, indicating improved, relevant interactions are taking place in-branch. Ultimately, this physical expansion is about customer acquisition and retention in a competitive landscape. While digital channels are efficient, physical branches provide a tangible point of contact that builds trust and loyalty, especially for significant life events like securing a mortgage or planning for retirement. JPMorgan's ability to arbitrage its terrestrial presence, much like digital players optimize SEO, allows it to increase leads in dense areas and drive productivity within branches by targeting high-value products. This comprehensive strategy, combining digital leadership with a strategic physical presence, aims to create a formidable competitive advantage. The branch expansion is poised to significantly impact customer acquisition and engagement by offering a blended experience that caters to diverse preferences. While 54% of bank customers primarily use mobile apps and 22% prefer online banking via PC, a substantial portion still values or occasionally utilizes physical branches. An ABA survey found that 9% of consumers still prefer visiting a branch, and critically, 63% of consumers desire one-on-one personal conversations with bank representatives. This highlights the enduring importance of the human touch, especially for complex financial needs. JPMorgan's strategy directly addresses this demand for personalized interaction. By opening new branches and renovating existing ones, the bank aims to increase its physical touchpoints, making it easier for customers to access in-person advice and services. The bank has already seen positive results, with more than 75% of customer balances held by regular branch visitors, indicating that these locations foster deeper, more engaged relationships. The addition of 1,100 new employees as part of this expansion further underscores the commitment to human-led service, moving closer to a goal of adding over 10,500 Consumer Bank team members by year-end. The segmented branch strategy is key to optimizing engagement. J.P. Morgan Financial Centers, for example, are designed to attract and retain high-net-worth clients who often require sophisticated wealth management and advisory services. These clients, who may prefer digital for routine tasks, still value the privacy and personal attention offered by a dedicated financial advisor in a premium setting. Similarly, Community Centers focus on building trust and providing financial literacy in underserved areas, offering workshops on budgeting, saving, and fraud prevention to both customers and non-customers alike. This community-centric approach can foster loyalty and bring new customers into the Chase ecosystem. Moreover, the physical presence acts as a powerful marketing channel. Approximately 25% of branded credit cards are sourced at the branch level, demonstrating the effectiveness of in-person interactions for product origination. By strategically placing branches in high-density urban hubs and fast-growing regions, JPMorgan can increase brand visibility and capture new business checking accounts for small business owners. This hybrid model ensures that whether a customer prefers digital convenience or in-person expertise, Chase can meet them where they are, ultimately driving higher customer satisfaction and deeper relationships that influence loyalty and the bottom line. The immediate impact of JPMorgan's aggressive expansion strategy is a significant increase in operational costs, as evidenced by the projected $105 billion expense guidance for 2026. This represents a $9 billion jump from 2025 and includes substantial investments not only in physical branches but also in AI-driven automation. While the market reacted negatively to this "expense shock," viewing it as a drag on short-term earnings, the bank frames these expenditures as crucial long-term investments designed to enhance efficiency and drive future profitability. The cost of opening new branches and renovating 1,700 locations is considerable, encompassing real estate, construction, technology upgrades, and staffing. However, JPMorgan's internal data suggests a relatively quick return on investment, with a 4-year break-even on new branch builds. This rapid payback period, coupled with the reported $160 billion in incremental deposits attributed to branch effectiveness, indicates that the physical network is a highly productive asset. The bank's ability to increase branch productivity from $120 million to $230 million in deposits per branch, significantly outperforming peers, underscores the efficiency of its branch strategy. From a profitability standpoint, the strategy aims to boost Net Interest Income (NII) and fee-based revenue. While the bank's 2026 NII guidance of $103 billion suggests a plateauing of interest income, the branch expansion is designed to drive future growth through increased deposit share and cross-selling of higher-margin products like mortgages, auto loans, and investment services. The Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) segment, which often benefits from in-person advisory services, was a standout performer in recent earnings, further validating the investment in high-touch client experiences. However, the strategy is not without risks. The $105 billion investment budget must yield immediate productivity gains and demonstrable returns to justify the expense. If these investments fail to translate into sustained revenue growth or operational efficiencies, the bank might face pressure to implement more aggressive cost-cutting measures. Furthermore, potential regulatory headwinds, such as a proposed 10% cap on credit card interest rates, could compress margins in the consumer division, making the need for diversified revenue streams and efficient operations even more critical. JPMorgan's robust $4.7 billion credit provision provides a buffer against potential credit losses, but a sustained recession would test its projected 3.4% net charge-off rate for credit cards. For investors, JPMorgan's branch expansion strategy presents a complex picture of short-term expense pressure versus long-term strategic positioning. The initial market reaction to the $105 billion expense guidance for 2026 highlights investor sensitivity to increased spending, especially when coupled with a projected plateauing of Net Interest Income. However, the bank's historical resilience and proactive investments suggest a fundamental belief in the long-term value of its diversified model. JPM is currently trading at $309.97, near its 52-week high of $337.25, reflecting underlying confidence despite recent expense concerns. The investment thesis hinges on JPMorgan's ability to execute its hybrid strategy effectively, leveraging both its digital leadership and expanded physical footprint to capture market share and deepen customer relationships. The bank's strong financial fundamentals, including a P/E ratio of 15.17 and a robust Return on Equity (ROE) of 15.9%, indicate a well-managed institution. Its dividend yield of 1.9% with a payout ratio of 28.2% also offers a compelling return for income-focused investors, demonstrating the bank's capacity to return capital even amidst heavy investment cycles. This strategy also has significant implications for the broader banking sector. JPMorgan's massive investment budget, nearly equal to the market capitalization of many mid-sized banks, underscores a widening "innovation gap." Smaller and regional banks may struggle to keep pace with the technological demands of modern banking and the cost of maintaining a competitive physical presence. This could lead to further consolidation in the industry, with larger players like JPMorgan continuing to absorb market share and talent, as seen with its acquisition of First Republic Bank assets. Conversely, the technology and AI sectors stand to benefit significantly from JPMorgan's commitment to spend billions on automation, highlighting the critical role of firms providing the infrastructure for the "bank of the future." Investors should closely monitor the realization of AI-related cost savings and the stability of consumer credit as the 2026 fiscal year progresses. While geopolitical warnings and regulatory threats add layers of uncertainty, JPMorgan's proactive positioning suggests a strategic move to solidify its market leadership and navigate a volatile financial landscape, making it a key bellwether for the industry. JPMorgan Chase's bold move to expand its physical branch network, even as it pours billions into AI and digital transformation, signals a clear vision for the future of banking: a powerful hybrid model. This isn't a retreat from digital, but rather a sophisticated integration of in-person expertise with cutting-edge technology. The bank is betting that true competitive advantage lies in offering customers seamless, personalized experiences across all channels, from mobile apps to concierge-style financial centers. This strategy, while costly in the short term, is designed to fortify JPMorgan's position as the dominant player in the U.S. financial landscape. By strategically expanding its reach into new markets and deepening relationships with high-value clients, the bank aims to drive sustainable revenue growth and enhance customer loyalty. For investors, the long-term narrative of market share gains and operational efficiencies, underpinned by a resilient "fortress" balance sheet, could outweigh the immediate "expense shock." title: Is It All One Big AI Trade? - J.P. Morgan
content:
Sharpen your knowledge with the latest wealth engagement news, market commentary and planning education. Access educational resources designed to help build and preserve your family legacy. Discover our approach, digital tools and community initiatives. AI’s reach extends well beyond technology, with diverse sectors showing strength and correlations evolving. Explore how this theme may influence portfolio strategy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the buzzword everywhere you go: The Nasdaq 100 is up +15% year to date (YTD), hyperscalers are expected to spend +$750 billion on capex (and that estimate seems to rise each earnings season), and LLM companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have increased revenues at an unbelievable pace. (Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate reportedly rocketed from $9 billion to $47 billion in about six months.) All of this is happening after two years of +20% S&P 500 returns, amid geopolitical conflicts, tariffs, the worst energy shock in history1 and consumer confidence near historic lows2 – so it’s understandable that many investors feel uneasy. A lot of attention this year has gone to chips and memory. Companies like Sandisk, TSMC, and SK Hynix are up sharply, and the semis index is up +39% YTD as semi net income is becoming a more significant contributor to the S&P 500. This line chart shows next-twelve-month net income as a percentage of the S&P 500 from 2020 through 2026, under the title "Semi net income has accelerated" with the subtitle "Next-twelve-month net income as a % of S&P 500." The vertical axis ranges from 4% at the bottom to 20% at the top in increments of 2%, and the horizontal axis spans years from '20 through '26 with annual markers. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: FactSet. Finance L.P. Data as of July 23, 2026." The line begins at approximately 5.5% in early 2020, moves in a narrow range between roughly 5% and 6% through 2020 and 2021, rises slightly to a local peak near 6.2% in mid-2021, then declines to a trough of approximately 4.5% in mid-2022. From late 2022 onward the line rises steadily and continuously, climbing from about 5% in early 2023 through roughly 6.5% by mid-2023, continuing upward to approximately 8% by early 2024, reaching about 9.5% by late 2024, and accelerating further to around 13% by mid-2025. The line then rises more steeply through late 2025, reaching approximately 15.5% to 16% before a sharp upward spike brings it to approximately 18.5% by the end of the series in 2026. But performance hasn’t been confined to a small corner of the market. Across the full AI value chain, the theme has been working. An analysis conducted of five different AI baskets containing 148 companies spanning the AI ecosystem (data centers, chips, memory, cooling, hyperscalers, electrification, software, etc.) revealed the following results: In other words, AI is showing up as a distributed theme across the value chain. AI and the AI supply chain are important drivers, but they’re not the only thing working. The most obvious non-AI driver this year has been geopolitics: With the conflict in the Middle East, energy is the top-performing sector in the S&P 500 so far this year, supported by elevated energy prices. That is an idiosyncratic driver but could reverse. Beyond that, there are more sustainable themes contributing to performance. Near-shoring remains top of mind, and industrials is a leading sector – driven not only by AI narratives, but also by a broader shift toward domestic and regional investment. Certain subsectors within healthcare and financials have performed well, as have certain materials. As Q2 earnings season ramps up, we expect 10 of 11 sectors to post positive earnings growth (six of those in double digits). Ultimately, AI is likely to be a success story for the entire market. If someone said, “I’m worried the email trade is taking over the market,” it might sound strange – the same goes for mobile. Those technological advancements became inseparable from corporate productivity and profitability. Over time, AI will become inseparable from the broader market as well. We’re just not there yet. The AI story is real and will likely be an integral part of portfolios in the years to come. But diversification, and the inherent importance it has for achieving your long-term goals, is still critical. One encouraging development over the past year is that when semis were “risk-off” (defined as one-month rolling compounded daily returns that are less than -5%), other sectors in the S&P 500 weren’t necessarily risk-off too. From a portfolio construction standpoint, this is positive: On days when the semi trade hasn’t worked, other parts of the portfolio have, on average, held up better. This bar chart shows the percentage of days each sector is risk-off when semiconductors are risk-off, year-to-date, under the title "Semis selloff ≠ market selloff" with the subtitle "% of days sector is risk-off when Semiconductors are risk off, Year-to-Date." The vertical axis ranges from 0% to 100% in increments of 10%, and the horizontal axis lists seven categories from left to right: Consumer Discretionary, Industrials, Financials, Consumer Staples, Health Care, Utilities, and Energy. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Note: Risk-off is defined as whenever 1-month rolling compounded daily returns are less than -5%." Each bar is labeled with its value at the top, and the bars are arranged in descending order: Consumer Discretionary is 86%, Industrials is 59%, Financials is 55%, Consumer Staples is 45%, Health Care is 45%, Utilities is 41%, and Energy is 18%. Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Note: Risk-off is defined as whenever 1-month rolling compounded daily returns are less than -5%. There’s also more breadth: YTD, the average stock is up more than the market-cap-weighted index. And importantly, the market is also not tech-blind – that is, not all tech is being treated equally. After years of nearly perfect correlation between semis and software, the two assets have become much less correlated over the past year as markets reassess who wins in an AI world. Once Claude Cowork came out, it became increasingly clear that parts of traditional software could be challenged as AI capabilities improve. This line chart shows the software 1-year rolling correlation to semiconductors from 2018 through 2026, under the title "Post Claude Cowork, Software and Semi correlations have plunged" with the subtitle "Software 1-year rolling correlation to Semiconductors." The vertical axis ranges from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1, and the horizontal axis spans years from '18 through '26 with annual markers. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 3, 2026." A vertical dashed reference line is positioned near the far right at 2026 and is annotated "Claude Cowork launch." The line begins at approximately 0.65 in early 2018, rises to a range of about 0.75 to 0.80 through 2018 and 2019 with a peak near 0.82, then moves lower before dropping to approximately 0.56 in early 2020. It then rises to about 0.90 across 2020 into early 2021, declines through 2021 to around 0.65 to 0.70, and then drops to approximately 0.45 in late 2021 into early 2022. The line then rises unevenly through 2022 and 2023 to roughly 0.85 in mid-2023, moves lower through 2024 to about 0.63, and rises again to approximately 0.80 in mid-to-late 2025. At the point of the "Claude Cowork launch" reference line at 2026, the line turns downward and falls from about 0.78 to approximately 0.29 by the end of the series. Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Another divergence emerging more recently is within the hyperscalers. Hyperscaler capex has been the engine of the AI trade for the past few years: Hyperscalers spend, the market rewards them for impressive growth and the broader AI universe benefits alongside them. But markets are increasingly wary of sustained high spend as these behemoths gradually draw down their cash flows. Alphabet’s earnings results are a clear example. Despite delivering impressive cloud revenue and a continued ballooning backlog, investors focused on the other side of the equation: Management again guided capex higher and reported its first negative quarter of free cash flow since its IPO. We’re seeing the market become more critical – and more discriminating – ­across hyperscalers as investors try to separate AI winners from losers. Long-term, the success (or failure) of the hyperscalers to generate an acceptable return on investment on their heavy capex investments will likely be correlated with the returns of the AI ecosystem. Ultimately, we think we’re only in the early innings of the AI tech cycle as AI has become much more useful in agentic form. Over time, AI’s reach will continue to grow and extend well beyond technology alone. That marks a increase of 24% sequentially. The reported value of JPMorgan’s stake in Opendoor increased from $2.01 million last December to $5.73 million in March 2026. BlackRock added 1.07 million Opendoor shares to its holdings in the first quarter, bringing the total to 63.45 million. That marks an increase of 1.7%. However, the reported value of BlackRock's stake in Opendoor has dropped from 135.37 million in December to $91.38 million in March. Opendoor shares dropped about 20% between January and March. Earlier this week, CEO Kaz Nejatian said he and his wife purchased $483,500 company shares, after a $1 million stock purchase last November. Other Opendoor investors, such as Pueo Keffer and Mike Alfred, are also loading up amid the dip following the company’s quarterly results last week. ASTS stock jumped nearly 3% on Wednesday, but is headed for a marginal weekly loss. The company still maintained its full-year revenue guidance of $150 million to $200 million, compared with consensus estimates of $181.13 million. Silicon Valley-based satellite communications consultant Tim Farrar said that the earnings call pointed to manufacturing and launch execution risks. He argued that AST SpaceMobile’s assumptions do not appear to support its target of having 45 satellites in orbit by year-end. Farrar said the company would likely need multiple high-frequency launches from Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, along with several additional Falcon 9 missions, to come close to that goal. He also questioned the company’s use of “satellite completion” milestones rather than clearer ready-for-shipment and ready-for-launch metrics. AST SpaceMobile’s deployment timeline has already faced scrutiny after last month’s failed BlueBird-7 mission aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn Mission-3 launch. BlueBird-7 separated from the rocket but failed to reach orbit after a second-stage anomaly. AST SpaceMobile previously said the satellite is expected to de-orbit and that insurance is expected to cover the loss. Wisniewski also said AST SpaceMobile has enough contracted launch capacity to meet its 2026 deployment goals and expects “a handful” of launches from both Blue Origin and SpaceX, or equivalent providers. New Street said that opportunity remains “largely underpriced.” The bullish stance comes as Rocket Lab aggressively builds out a vertically integrated space and defense platform spanning reusable rockets, hypersonic testing, defense payloads, spacecraft manufacturing and orbital infrastructure. During the company’s recent quarterly earnings call, Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck highlighted the company’s exposure to national security and defense programs, including the Pentagon’s MACH-TB hypersonic initiative and Golden Dome-related Space interceptor opportunities. Rocket Lab also disclosed a record $2.2 billion backlog, while confirming that customer demand for its upcoming reusable Neutron rocket remains strong ahead of the vehicle’s expected first launch later this year. The company also announced a major 20-launch Haste hypersonics contract, alongside a separate Neutron agreement, the largest launch contract in Rocket Lab’s history. Space stocks have been riding SpaceX’s IPO buzz, with the firm targeting a mid-2026 IPO that could value the Elon Musk-led company between $1.75 trillion and $2 trillion, potentially making it one of the largest public listings in market history. Markets have increasingly focused on SpaceX’s expansion beyond rockets into AI infrastructure, satellite broadband, direct-to-device communications and orbital data-center ambitions. The enthusiasm accelerated further after reports of Google being in talks with SpaceX for a potential rocket-launch deal for orbital AI data centers. SpaceX has also recently announced agreements involving Anthropic and filed applications to launch up to one million satellites supporting future orbital infrastructure. Investors have additionally focused on the possibility that a future SpaceX IPO could trigger major passive ETF inflows following accelerated index inclusion rule changes across Nasdaq, S&P and FTSE Russell. New Street also identified EchoStar as a direct proxy play on SpaceX. The firm pointed to EchoStar’s 2.2% ownership stake in SpaceX after the xAI merger, saying that a future SpaceX IPO at a higher valuation could create “meaningful upside” for SATS shares. The brokerage also highlighted EchoStar’s growing importance in direct-to-device satellite connectivity infrastructure. Recently, the FCC approved EchoStar’s sale of 65 megahertz of nationwide spectrum to SpaceX for Starlink’s direct-to-device offerings. The FCC said that the deal would boost America’s leadership in satellite-to-smartphone connectivity, while accelerating wireless infrastructure. New Street also turned bullish on Viasat, saying that the company’s ownership of the world’s “largest band of global MSS spectrum” is not being reflected in the current share price. The brokerage believes that Viasat’s spectrum position could become more valuable as satellite broadband, direct-to-device communications and orbit connectivity markets continue expanding globally. The call comes shortly after Viasat successfully launched its ViaSat-3 Flight 3 satellite aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket last month. The satellite is expected to add more than 1 terabit per second of throughput capacity across the Asia-Pacific region as part of Viasat’s broader multi-orbit connectivity strategy. Viasat said the constellation can support aviation connectivity, maritime broadband, government and defense communications, business internet services and rural broadband expansion globally. Meanwhile, New Street assigned ‘Sell’ ratings to Planet Labs and Telesat. For Planet Labs, the brokerage said that the company remains “well positioned with tier-2 countries” but expressed concerns that the valuation already reflects much of that opportunity. For Telesat, New Street warned that the rapid rise in satellite capacity from both Starlink and Amazon could pressure pricing across the industry and potentially lead the company to miss future revenue expectations. title: What Does JPMorgan's Latest Dividend Declaration Signify - Kavout | AI
content: JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) continues to demonstrate its financial resilience and dedication to rewarding shareholders, with the latest quarterly dividend declaration of $1.50 per share reinforcing a bullish outlook for the banking giant. This consistent capital return strategy, backed by a fortress balance sheet and diversified revenue streams, makes JPM a compelling consideration for income-focused investors and those seeking stability in the financial sector. JPMorgan Chase's Board of Directors recently declared a quarterly dividend of $1.50 per share on its common stock, announced on May 18, 2026. This dividend is scheduled to be paid on July 31, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on July 6, 2026. This declaration is not merely a routine announcement; it serves as a strong indicator of the bank's robust financial standing and its confidence in future earnings, especially following a period of strategic capital allocation. The $1.50 per share dividend maintains the level set in previous quarters, including the one paid on April 30, 2026, which had an ex-dividend date of April 6, 2026. This consistency is a hallmark of JPM's approach to shareholder returns, which has seen the dividend per share grow by 15.9% year-over-year in fiscal year 2025. Such a track record, with 14 consecutive years of dividend increases through various economic cycles, speaks volumes about the sustainability of its payout. For investors, a stable and growing dividend from a financial titan like JPMorgan Chase offers a tangible return on investment, particularly in an environment where income generation remains a priority. The current trailing twelve months (TTM) dividend payout for JPM stands at $6.00, translating to a dividend yield of 1.9% based on the current share price of $306.74. This yield, while slightly below the industry average of 2.3% as noted by some analysts, is underpinned by a conservative payout ratio of 29.2%, leaving ample room for future increases and reinvestment into the business. JPMorgan Chase's TTM dividend payout ratio of 29.2% is a critical metric that highlights the bank's prudent capital management and strong financial health. This ratio indicates that less than a third of the bank's earnings are distributed as dividends, leaving a substantial portion for reinvestment, debt reduction, or share repurchases. For a financial institution, a conservative payout ratio is particularly important as it provides a buffer against unexpected economic downturns and regulatory changes, ensuring the stability of future payouts. This conservative approach is further supported by JPM's robust earnings per share (EPS) of $21.12 for the trailing twelve months. With the $6.00 annualized dividend, the earnings comfortably cover the payout, reinforcing the sustainability of the dividend stream. In fact, Simply Wall St analysts project the dividend to remain well covered by earnings, with a forecast payout ratio of 28% in three years, even as EPS is expected to grow by 23% over the next three years. This forward-looking stability provides a strong foundation for income-seeking investors. Beyond the payout ratio, JPM's overall financial strength is evident in its substantial capital base. As of December 31, 2025, the firm reported $4.4 trillion in assets and $362 billion in stockholders' equity. Chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon has consistently emphasized the bank's "fortress balance sheet," which includes $291 billion in CET1 capital and $1.5 trillion in cash and marketable securities. This significant excess capital and robust liquidity enable the bank to not only sustain its dividend but also to navigate various market conditions, including the Federal Reserve's stress tests, which JPM has consistently cleared. JPMorgan Chase's capital allocation strategy extends beyond just dividends, encompassing significant share repurchase programs that further enhance shareholder value. On July 1, 2025, the firm's Board of Directors authorized a new common share repurchase program of $50 billion. This authorization, used at management's discretion, complements the dividend strategy by reducing the number of outstanding shares, thereby boosting EPS and potentially the stock price over time. The combination of a consistent dividend and an active share repurchase program signals a comprehensive approach to capital return. This dual strategy is particularly attractive to investors, as it offers both immediate income and potential capital appreciation. Jamie Dimon highlighted this, stating that the intended dividend increase and the new share repurchase program represent a "sustainable level of capital distribution" supported by strong financial performance. This commitment is crucial for maintaining investor confidence, especially given the firm's leadership position in investment banking, consumer banking, and asset management. Furthermore, JPM's strategic investments in its core businesses and expansion initiatives demonstrate a forward-looking approach to growth. The bank plans to open more than 500 new branches by 2027, with 150 already established in 2024, despite the rise of digital banking. This initiative, alongside its expansion of digital retail banking in Germany by early 2026 and across the European Union, aims to tailor its network to client needs and boost cross-selling. These growth drivers, coupled with a rebound in investment banking activity, are expected to underpin future earnings, providing a solid foundation for continued capital returns. JPMorgan Chase's current valuation metrics present a nuanced picture for investors, balancing its strong fundamentals with its recent stock performance. The stock is currently trading at $306.74, reflecting a modest gain of +0.12% today. Over the past year, JPM shares have traded within a 52-week range of $260.31 to $337.25, indicating that the stock is currently positioned towards the higher end of this range. From a valuation perspective, JPM's TTM Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 14.52. This is slightly below the industry average of 14.95x as noted by Zacks Investment Research in September 2025, suggesting that the stock might not be excessively overvalued compared to its peers. However, Simply Wall St noted in May 2026 that JPM's forward 12-month earnings multiple of 15.39x compared to the industry's 14.95x indicates a "stretched valuation." This discrepancy highlights the importance of considering both trailing and forward-looking metrics. Despite some concerns about valuation, analyst sentiment remains predominantly positive. Of 28 analysts covering JPM, 12 rate it a Buy, 14 a Hold, and only 2 a Sell. The average target price is $328.00, which implies a potential upside of approximately 7% from the current price. This consensus suggests that while the stock has performed well, there is still room for appreciation, driven by resilient credit quality, updated investor day guidance, and generally constructive views on large diversified banks. The firm's robust Return on Equity (ROE) of 16.3% and revenue growth of 3.3% (FY2025 YoY) further underscore its operational efficiency and ability to generate profits, making the current valuation potentially justifiable for long-term holders. While JPMorgan Chase presents a compelling investment case, particularly for dividend-focused investors, it is crucial to consider the inherent risks and future opportunities that could influence its performance. One significant opportunity lies in the rebound of its Investment Banking (IB) business. After a slowdown in global deal-making in early 2022 due to geopolitical tensions and inflation, JPM's total IB fees in the Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) segment rose 36% year-over-year in 2024. The healthy IB pipeline and an active M&A market are expected to drive stronger growth once macroeconomic conditions stabilize, with Douglas Petno, co-CEO of CIB, projecting low-double-digit year-over-year growth in IB fees for Q3 2025. However, the bank faces potential headwinds related to interest rate policy and net interest income (NII). While management projected NII of $95.5 billion for 2025, up more than 3% year-over-year, lower rates are expected to hurt the metric in 2026 as the Federal Reserve navigates rate policy. JPM's balance sheet is highly asset-sensitive, meaning declining rates could compress NII. This is a common challenge for large banks, with peers like Bank of America and Citigroup also anticipating modest NII compression over the medium term. On the risk side, asset quality deterioration remains a watch point. While JPM recorded negative provisions in 2021, a substantial rise in provisions occurred in subsequent years due to a worsening macroeconomic outlook. Management projects the card net charge-off rate to be 3.6% for 2025. However, lower rates could support asset quality by easing debt-service burdens and improving borrower solvency. JPM's extensive suite of services, from consumer banking to wealth management, diversifies its revenue streams, strengthening its resilience against sector-specific downturns and providing a buffer against these risks. JPMorgan Chase's consistent dividend declarations, including the latest $1.50 per share payout on July 31, 2026, underscore its financial strength and commitment to shareholders. The bank's conservative payout ratio of 29.2% and robust capital position provide a solid foundation for sustainable income. While valuation requires careful consideration, JPM's strategic growth initiatives and diversified business model position it well to navigate future economic shifts and continue delivering value. title: Is it all one big AI trade? - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Artificial intelligence is the buzzword everywhere you go: The NASDAQ 100 is up +15% year-to-date, hyperscalers are expected to spend +$750 billion on capex (and that estimate seems to rise each earnings season), and LLM companies, such as Anthropic and OpenAI, have increased revenues at an unbelievable pace (Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate reportedly rocketed from $9 billion to $47 billion in about six months). All of this is happening after two years of +20% S&P 500 returns, amid geopolitical conflicts, tariffs, the worst energy shock in history1 and consumer confidence near historic lows2—so it’s understandable that many investors feel uneasy. A lot of attention this year has gone to chips and memory. Companies like Sandisk, TSMC and SK Hynix are up sharply, and the semis index is up +39% year-to-date as their net income is becoming a more significant contributor to the S&P 500. But performance hasn’t been confined to a small corner of the market. Across the full AI value chain, the theme has been working. An analysis conducted of five different AI baskets containing 148 companies spanning the AI ecosystem (data centers, chips, memory, cooling, hyperscalers, electrification, software, etc.) revealed the following results: In other words, AI is showing up as a distributed theme across the value chain. AI and the AI supply chain are an important driver, but they’re not the only thing working. The most obvious non-AI driver this year has been geopolitics: With the conflict in the Middle East, energy is the top-performing sector in the S&P 500 so far this year, supported by elevated energy prices. That’s an idiosyncratic driver but could reverse. Beyond that, there are more sustainable themes contributing to performance. Nearshoring remains top of mind, and industrials is a leading sector—driven not only by AI narratives, but also by a broader shift toward domestic and regional investment. Certain sub-sectors within healthcare and financials have performed well, as have certain materials. As Q2 earnings season ramps up, we expect 10 of 11 sectors to post positive earnings growth (six of those in double digits). Ultimately, AI is likely to be a success story for the entire market. If someone said, “I’m worried the email trade is taking over the market,” it may sound strange—same for “mobile.” Those are technological advancements that became inseparable from corporate productivity and profitability. Over time, AI will become inseparable from the broader market as well. We’re just not there yet. The AI story is real and will likely be an integral part of portfolios in the years to come. But diversification, and the inherent importance it has for achieving your long-term goals, is still critical. One encouraging development over the past year is that when semiconductors were “risk-off” (defined as one-month rolling compounded daily returns that are less than -5%), other sectors in the S&P 500 weren’t necessarily risk-off too. From a portfolio construction standpoint, this is positive: On days when the semiconductor trade hasn’t worked, other parts of the portfolio have, on average, held up better. Another divergence emerging more recently is within the hyperscalers. Hyperscaler capex has been the engine of the AI trade for the last few years: Hyperscalers spend, the market rewards them for impressive growth, and the broader AI universe benefits alongside them. But markets are increasingly wary of sustained high spend as these behemoths gradually draw down their cashflows. Alphabet’s earnings results are a clear example. Despite delivering impressive cloud revenue and a continued ballooning backlog, investors focused on the other side of the equation: Management again guided capex higher and reported its first negative quarter of free cash flow since its initial public offering (IPO). We’re seeing the market become more critical—and more discriminating—across hyperscalers as investors try to separate AI winners from losers. Long-term, the success (or failure) of the hyperscalers to generate an acceptable return on investment on their heavy capex investments, will likely be correlated with the returns of the AI ecosystem. Ultimately, we think we’re only in the early innings of the AI tech cycle as AI has become much more useful in agentic form. Over time, AI’s reach will continue to grow and extend well beyond technology alone. title: IRS boss Frank Bisignano has been accused of corporate spying — here’s what his old employer JPMorgan thinks - New York Post
content: See more of our coverage in your search results. Frank Bisignano allegedly spied on colleagues and misused company funds during his stint at JPMorgan Chase more than a decade ago. Those, at least, were the most sensational accusations in a lengthy Wall Street Journal report this week on Donald Trump’s IRS chief, who spent years at the big bank in various senior positions including co-chief operating officer working directly under CEO Jamie Dimon. Given the gravity of the story, I called JPMorgan, which had previously called Bisignano “a trusted adviser for years who we have known for decades and who is distinguished for his grit and determination. We applaud his service to our country both at the Social Security Administration and the IRS.” I then spoke to a senior JPMorgan executive who has firsthand knowledge of these more-than-a-decade-old claims. He said the “bank looked into the allegations of spying and misuse of funds and found no evidence of wrongdoing.” A spokeswoman for the Journal said: “Our reporting is accurate, thoroughly vetted, and backed by multiple knowledgeable sources. We stand behind the story.” Full disclosure: On The Money is a column in the New York Post, which shares a corporate owner with the Wall Street Journal. Back in the day, your humble correspondent spent years at the Journal reporting on Wall Street. That’s how I got to know the players involved in this story – from Bisignano to Dimon to Wells Fargo CEO Charles Scharf, who figures prominently in it – and also the president himself when he was a real estate mogul and reality TV star. In other words, I have no horse in this race other than having to cover something, which if true is a pretty big story. Consider, Bisignano now runs both the Internal Revenue Service and the Social Security Administration, which the Journal rightly says “puts him atop of two government organizations that store vast reams of sensitive financial data about every taxpayer.” Bisignano was brought on to apply his Wall Street knowledge to streamline government and make it more efficient for taxpayers. All of which makes this part of the story all the more serious: “More than a decade ago, he was co-chief operating officer at JPMorgan Chase, another perch that gave him visibility and authority over every part of a massive financial institution. At the bank, people familiar with the matter said, he spied on fellow executives—using his authority over the security department and position to access sensitive information and internal communications without an apparent business justification.” One of those executives was Scharf, then Dimon’s consumer bank chief, the paper said. There were other alleged misdeeds cited in the piece, some of which seem like normal grousing about a guy who, if you know Bisignano, can be a little rough around the edges. That’s despite the fact that at least one of those allegations also involves something pretty serious: the alleged “use of company resources for his own benefit, including allegations Bisignano misused the corporate jet for personal purposes, people familiar with the matter said.” Again, using the corporate jet for personal reasons is the easiest way to get jammed up on Wall Street, which is why I was a little shocked to read that part of the story. Knowing what I know about Bisignano, my first reaction is that he’s probably too careful to do something that dumb that would put him at odds with a legendary control freak like Dimon. That allegation, according to the bank executive who asked not to be quoted by name, was investigated as well and JPM “found no evidence,” the executive said. Bisignano, through a lawyer, denied that charge as well as the spying allegation. I asked Scharf about the mess. He tells me that he and Bisignano are friends, and that he has heard rumblings about spying in the past. “All I know is what I’ve seen and I’ve never seen any spying,” he said. Scharf, who left JPM in 2012, said he and Bisignano spoke after the story ran and Bisignano denied the matter. In fact the two “joked” about it. One possible explanation of what went down came from another former colleague who explained Bisignano’s role at JPM this way: “Bisignano was in charge of compliance (as co-COO) ALL senior managers were told to work with compliance, the in-house police in charge of monitoring emails internally as well as externally making sure we all were complying with firm policy. It’s now known as tech/opps but back in the day, those functions were known as back office. Frank was given the job by Jamie and made something of it. They looked at everything we did.” Sign up to receive On The Money by Charlie Gasparino in your inbox every Thursday. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Again, the Journal cited multiple sources; Bisignano through his attorney denied each allegation. And remember, all this happened more than a decade ago. Since leaving JPM in 2013, Bisignano has had a pretty remarkable career as CEO of payments processor First Data, and later with Fiserv after the two merged and just before he joined Team Trump as a change agent to reform two institutions known for their bureaucratic bloat. To address those issues he recently hired another JPMorgan executive, Vince LaPadula as his No. 2 at the IRS. Before his exit from the big bank, LaPadula tells me he sat down with Dimon and asked if he should work for Bisignano. “Jamie told me absolutely… he’s Mr. Fix It.” One other question I have is why am I reading all of this now? title: Former JP Morgan banker allegedly pushed to keep Epstein as client - upi.com
content: July 23 (UPI) -- Former JP Morgan Chase investment banking boss Jes Staley pushed the bank to keep Jeffrey Epstein as a client despite red flags surrounding the late sex offender, House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., said Thursday. "It appears that within JPMorgan there were flags -- red flags -- about Epstein, but Mr. Staley is on record defending Epstein and encouraging JPMorgan to keep him as a client," Comer told CNBC outside Staley's closed-door testimony before the committee. "So we have a lot of questions about that." Staley was Epstein's private banker at JP Morgan and stayed friends with him for years. "If it weren't for banks and bankers like Jes Staley, then Jeffrey Epstein would not have been able to continue to commit these crimes against women," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said in a press conference Thursday. "He would not have continued to do some of the things that he did. But it was because of these banks that he was able to do so." More than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein appear in the files released by the Department of Justice last year. Some include Staley describing their friendship as "profound" and calling Epstein "family." "We have email documentation that in 2010 he was requesting and interacting with Jeffrey Epstein to procure women that he had sexual encounters with, and when he was asked in [the committee hearing] what happened and to describe those encounters, he could not recall," Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a press conference. Staley became CEO of Barclays in 2015 but resigned in 2021. He was banned from the British financial industry for misleading regulators about his friendship with Epstein. Britain's Financial Conduct Authority conducted the investigation, and Staley appealed the ban in court, which meant a public hearing, The Guardian reported. Staley admitted to having sex with an Epstein staff member in New York, but said that he would describe the encounter as "consensual." The judges agreed with the FCA. Staley also lost $24 million of pay and bonuses from Barclays as a result of the ruling. Staley said in 2020, "Obviously I thought I knew him well, and I didn't," and "with hindsight of what we all know now, I deeply regret having had any relationship with Jeffrey Epstein." JPMorgan agreed in 2023 to pay $290 million to settle with Epstein's victims and $75 million to resolve a separate case brought by the U.S. Virgin Islands. The bank later reached a confidential settlement with Staley. Democrats on the committee said that JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon's name didn't come up in the testimony.
